claim: Fusion of mitochondrial outer membranes involves large GTPases called mitofusins.
source: Fusion of mitochondrial outer membranes is crucial for proper organelle function and involves large GTPases called mitofusins.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: Cycles of GTP hydrolysis induce progressive formation of a docking ring structure around extended areas of contact between mitochondria.
source: We find that cycles of GTP hydrolysis induce progressive formation of a docking ring structure around extended areas of contact.
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-ET observations and time-course experiments with GMP-PNP shown in Figures 2, 4, and 5.

claim: Further GTP hydrolysis triggers local outer membrane fusion at the periphery of the contact region.
source: Further GTP hydrolysis triggers local outer membrane fusion at the periphery of the contact region.
evidence: This is supported by the observation of fusion pores at the edge of docking rings (Figure 6) and GMP-PNP inhibition experiments.

claim: Protein and lipid trafficking mainly involves SNAREs that are expressed on all intracellular compartments undergoing fusion except peroxisomes and mitochondria.
source: Protein and lipid trafficking mainly involves SNAREs (Soluble N-ethyl maleimide sensitive factor Attachment protein Receptors) that are expressed on all intracellular compartments undergoing fusion except peroxisomes and mitochondria (Cai et al., 2007; Escobar-Henriques and Anton, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mitochondria constitute a remarkably dynamic network with an organization and ultra-structure that is regulated by fusion and fission of mitochondrial outer and inner membranes.
source: Mitochondria constitute a remarkably dynamic network with an organization and ultra-structure that is regulated by fusion and fission of mitochondrial outer and inner membranes (Labbé et al., 2014; Westermann, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Fusion and fission are crucial for all mitochondrial functions including oxidative phosphorylation, calcium signalling, apoptosis and lipid metabolism.
source: Fusion and fission are crucial for all mitochondrial functions including oxidative phosphorylation, calcium signalling, apoptosis and lipid metabolism.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Defects in mitochondrial fusion and fission are associated with numerous pathologies and severe neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Defects in mitochondrial fusion and fission are associated with numerous pathologies and severe neurodegenerative diseases (Dorn, 2013; Liesa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mitochondrial fusion and fission both depend on large GTPases of the Dynamin-Related Protein (DRP) family.
source: Mitochondrial fusion and fission both depend on large GTPases of the Dynamin-Related Protein (DRP) family (Labbé et al., 2014; Low and Löwe, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: To promote fission, soluble DRPs assemble into spirals around membrane compartments.
source: To promote fission, soluble DRPs assemble into spirals around membrane compartments.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: GTP hydrolysis causes the spirals to constrict, reducing the diameter of the compartments, ultimately followed by their separation.
source: GTP hydrolysis causes the spirals to constrict, reducing the diameter of the compartments, ultimately followed by their separation (Bui and Shaw, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Mitofusins and OPA1 mediate fusion of the mitochondrial outer and inner membranes, respectively.
source: Among the three families of transmembrane DRPs implicated in fusion, Mitofusins and OPA1 mediate fusion of the mitochondrial outer and inner membranes, respectively, whereas atlastins promote homotypic fusion of ER tubules (McNew et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Atlastins promote homotypic fusion of ER tubules.
source: Among the three families of transmembrane DRPs implicated in fusion, Mitofusins and OPA1 mediate fusion of the mitochondrial outer and inner membranes, respectively, whereas atlastins promote homotypic fusion of ER tubules (McNew et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: GTP binding and hydrolysis participate in trans auto-oligomerization of atlastins and OPA1 through their respective GTPase domains.
source: GTP binding and hydrolysis participate in trans auto-oligomerization of atlastins and OPA1 through their respective GTPase domains (Rujiviphat et al., 2012; Klemm et al., 2011; Byrnes et al., 2013; DeVay et al., 2009; Meglei and McQuibban, 2009; Moss et al., 2011; Saini et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Homotypic tethering of ER and mitochondrial inner membranes is accompanied by conformational rearrangements of the DRPs that are thought to trigger subsequent fusion of lipid bilayers.
source: The resulting homotypic tethering of ER and mitochondrial inner membranes is accompanied by conformational rearrangements of the DRPs that are thought to trigger subsequent fusion of lipid bilayers.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from prior work on DRPs.

claim: Mitofusins may promote outer membrane tethering and fusion through processes of oligomerization and conformational rearrangement similar to BDLP.
source: Based on structural insights gained from BDLP (Bacterial Dynamin-Like Protein) (Low and Löwe, 2006; Low et al., 2009), a close relative of the yeast mitofusin Fzo1, mitofusins may promote outer membrane tethering and fusion through similar processes of oligomerization and conformational rearrangement (Cohen et al., 2011; Escobar-Henriques and Anton, 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural similarity to BDLP, supported by citations.

claim: BDLP is a close relative of the yeast mitofusin Fzo1.
source: Based on structural insights gained from BDLP (Bacterial Dynamin-Like Protein) (Low and Löwe, 2006; Low et al., 2009), a close relative of the yeast mitofusin Fzo1, mitofusins may promote outer membrane tethering and fusion through similar processes of oligomerization and conformational rearrangement (Cohen et al., 2011; Escobar-Henriques and Anton, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: DRPs are characterized by their ability to assemble into higher-order macromolecular structures.
source: As seen with spirals formed during membrane scission, DRPs are characterized by their ability to assemble into higher-order macromolecular structures (Ingerman et al., 2005; Low et al., 2009; Mears and Hinshaw, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Whether DRPs participate in the formation of higher-order structures during membrane attachment and fusion is unknown.
source: Whether DRPs participate in the formation of such structures during membrane attachment and fusion is unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap motivating the study.

claim: The precise orchestration of events from the initial attachment of membranes to their ultimate fusion and the requirement for GTP binding and hydrolysis during these steps is elusive.
source: In particular, the precise orchestration of events from the initial attachment of membranes to their ultimate fusion and the requirement for GTP binding and hydrolysis during these steps is elusive.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The in vitro mitochondrial fusion assay allows distinction between discrete steps of the mitochondrial fusion process (i.e. attachment, fusion of outer membranes and fusion of inner membranes).
source: The in vitro mitochondrial fusion assay (Figure 1A) allows us to distinguish between discrete steps of the mitochondrial fusion process (i.e. attachment, fusion of outer membranes and fusion of inner membranes) (Hoppins et al., 2009; Meeusen et al., 2006, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work establishing the assay.

claim: Incubation at 4°C for 10 min promotes mitofusin-dependent attachment.
source: Purified mitochondria from wild-type yeast cells were brought into contact by centrifugation and were incubated at 4°C for 10 min to promote mitofusin-dependent attachment (Meeusen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Subsequent incubation for 45 min at 25°C allows fusion of outer membranes but not inner membranes unless energy is regenerated.
source: Subsequent incubation for 45 min at 25°C allows fusion of outer membranes but not inner membranes (Figure 1A; top) unless energy is regenerated (Meeusen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Fusion reactions recurrently yielded 6 to 8% intermediates with fused outer membranes.
source: Consistent with this, fusion reactions recurrently yielded 6 to 8% intermediates with fused outer membranes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Prolonged incubation of centrifuged mitochondria at 4°C decreases fusion of outer membranes but stabilizes attached intermediates.
source: Prolonged incubation of centrifuged mitochondria at 4°C (Figure 1A; bottom) decreases fusion of outer membranes but stabilizes attached intermediates (Cohen et al., 2011) with approximately 25% of mitochondria in close contact (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Approximately 25% of mitochondria are in close contact after prolonged incubation at 4°C.
source: Prolonged incubation of centrifuged mitochondria at 4°C (Figure 1A; bottom) decreases fusion of outer membranes but stabilizes attached intermediates (Cohen et al., 2011) with approximately 25% of mitochondria in close contact (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 79% of the contact areas were organized as regions where opposing outer membranes approached one another to a distance of 1–3 nm.
source: 79% of the contact areas were organized as regions where opposing outer membranes approached one another to a distance ds of 1–3 nm (Figure 2A, green bracket; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), without observable density between the membranes.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The contact areas displayed an average surface of 22,600 ± 3100 nm² with flattened outer membranes.
source: The contact areas displayed an average surface of 22,600 ± 3100 nm² with flattened outer membranes, prompting us to term this state 'docked' intermediates (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of cryo-ET data shown in Figure 2.

claim: At the edges of the contact areas, where the distance between outer membranes reached 6–9 nm, defined protein densities were detected between the two outer membranes.
source: At the edges of the contact areas, where the distance dl between outer membranes reached 6–9 nm (Figure 2A, blue brackets; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), we detected defined protein densities between the two outer membranes (Figure 2A; yellow arrows).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Contact areas are delimited by a dense ring-like structure, termed the docking ring.
source: Tomographic reconstruction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and 3D rendered volumes (Figure 2B) of mitochondria revealed that contact areas are delimited by a dense ring-like structure, termed the docking ring (Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by 3D reconstruction of cryo-ET data shown in Figure 2B and Video 1.

claim: The remaining 21% of attached mitochondria had contact areas that were smaller (6900 ± 1700 nm²) with an average distance of 6.7 ± 0.5 nm between outer membranes.
source: Contact areas of the remaining 21% of attached mitochondria were smaller (6900 ± 1700 nm²) with an average distance of 6.7 ± 0.5 nm between outer membranes (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of cryo-ET data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In tethered intermediates, there were clear densities between the apposed outer membranes over the complete contact area.
source: In contrast to docked intermediates, there were clear densities between the apposed outer membranes over the complete contact area (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The density in tethered intermediates appeared to consist of more or less regular repeats of globular protein units.
source: Frequently, this density appeared to consist of more or less regular repeats of globular protein units (Figure 3B; red arrows).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The globular protein units in tethered intermediates have an average spacing of 4.6 ± 0.7 nm.
source: These units, with an average spacing of 4.6 ± 0.7 nm (n = 13), occasionally extended two protrusions toward each membrane (Figure 3B; inserted zoom).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of cryo-ET data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The globular protein units occasionally extended two protrusions toward each membrane.
source: These units, with an average spacing of 4.6 ± 0.7 nm (n = 13), occasionally extended two protrusions toward each membrane (Figure 3B; inserted zoom).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Homotypic attachment of outer membranes and their subsequent fusion depends on the GTPase activity of mitofusins.
source: As the homotypic attachment of outer membranes and their subsequent fusion depends on the GTPase activity of mitofusins (Cohen et al., 2011; Koshiba et al., 2004), we assessed the impact of GTP hydrolysis on the formation of the tethered and docked intermediates.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Treatment with GMP-PNP resulted in only 14% of mitochondria forming contacts reminiscent of docked intermediates with significantly smaller contact areas.
source: In contrast to non-treated samples, only 14% of mitochondria formed contacts reminiscent of docked intermediates and with significantly smaller contact areas (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data and quantitative analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: In 86% of attached mitochondria treated with GMP-PNP, the outer membranes were 6.3 ± 0.2 nm apart.
source: In the remaining 86% of attached mitochondria, the outer membranes were 6.3 ± 0.2 nm apart (Figure 4A, blue bracket).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Densities between apposed membranes in GMP-PNP-treated samples showed frequent repeats of 3–4 nm globular structures with regular spacing of 4.3 ± 0.6 nm.
source: Densities were observed between apposed membranes with frequent repeats of 3–4 nm globular structures with, occasionally, two protrusions extending towards each membrane (Figure 4A, inserted zoom and Figure 4B, red arrows). These densities and their regular spacing (4.3 ± 0.6 nm; n = 24) were strikingly similar to those seen in wild-type tethered intermediates (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The sub-population observed upon treatment with GMP-PNP displayed features essentially identical to the tethered intermediates seen in wild-type conditions.
source: Moreover, among the attached intermediates we identified (Table 1), this sub-population observed upon treatment with GMP-PNP displayed features that were essentially identical to the tethered intermediates seen in wild-type conditions both in terms of morphology (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A; Video 2) and statistics (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis of cryo-ET data shown in Figure 4 and supplementary figures.

claim: Inhibition of GTP hydrolysis induces the accumulation of tethered mitochondria at the expense of docked intermediates.
source: These observations suggest that inhibition of GTP hydrolysis induces the accumulation of tethered mitochondria at the expense of docked intermediates (21% tethered intermediates in wild-type conditions against 86% upon GMP-PNP treatment).
evidence: This is inferred from the quantitative comparison of wild-type and GMP-PNP-treated samples.

claim: Docked intermediates were predominantly found when GMP-PNP was added 10, 20 or 40 min after centrifugation.
source: Docked intermediates were predominantly found when GMP-PNP was added 10, 20 or 40 min after centrifugation (Figure 5B, blue squares), indicating that the ring had been already formed and that it was not dissolved by GMP-PNP.
evidence: This is supported by time-course experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The docking ring is not dissolved by GMP-PNP once formed.
source: Docked intermediates were predominantly found when GMP-PNP was added 10, 20 or 40 min after centrifugation (Figure 5B, blue squares), indicating that the ring had been already formed and that it was not dissolved by GMP-PNP.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that docked intermediates persist after GMP-PNP addition.

claim: Addition of GMP-PNP prior to or immediately after centrifugation resulted in strong accumulation of tethered intermediates.
source: In contrast, addition of GMP-PNP prior to or immediately after centrifugation resulted in strong accumulation of tethered intermediates (Figure 5B, red circles), while docked intermediates were suppressed.
evidence: This is supported by time-course experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Addition of GMP-PNP two minutes after centrifugation resulted in equal proportions of tethered and docked intermediates.
source: Strikingly, addition of GMP-PNP two minutes after centrifugation resulted in equal proportions of tethered and docked intermediates (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by time-course experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Tethering precedes docking.
source: These observations demonstrate not only that tethering precedes docking, but also that transition from one state to the other is controlled by GTP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the time-course experiments showing the sequential appearance of intermediates.

claim: Transition from tethering to docking is controlled by GTP hydrolysis.
source: These observations demonstrate not only that tethering precedes docking, but also that transition from one state to the other is controlled by GTP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the GMP-PNP experiments showing that inhibition of GTP hydrolysis blocks the transition.

claim: The tethered intermediate with its repeating globular protein densities represents an early stage of the mitochondrial outer membrane fusion process.
source: Consequently, the tethered intermediate with its repeating globular protein densities represents an early stage of the mitochondrial outer membrane fusion process.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequential order of intermediates established by time-course experiments.

claim: GTP hydrolysis allows the tethered stage to evolve towards the docked state with the docking ring.
source: GTP hydrolysis then allows this stage to evolve towards the docked state with the docking ring.
evidence: This is inferred from the GMP-PNP experiments showing that GTP hydrolysis is required for the transition.

claim: A discrete category of intermediates was detected with apposed membrane regions sandwiching protein densities identical to those in tethered intermediates and regions reminiscent of docked contact areas.
source: Consistent with this, a discrete category of intermediates was detected among the mixed population of tethered and docked intermediates when GMP-PNP was added two minutes after centrifugation. This category was characterized by apposed membrane regions sandwiching protein densities identical to those in tethered intermediates and regions reminiscent of docked contact areas where outer membranes approached to within less than 3 nm (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Video 3.

claim: The hybrid category of attached mitochondria probably represents a transition state from mitochondrial tethering towards mitochondrial docking.
source: This hybrid category of attached mitochondria probably represents a transition state from mitochondrial tethering towards mitochondrial docking.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of intermediates with features of both tethered and docked states.

claim: The proportion of docked intermediates increases when outer membrane fusion can proceed but decreases when fusion is inhibited.
source: The proportion of docked intermediates increases when outer membrane fusion can proceed but decreases when fusion is inhibited, as we showed by inhibiting GTP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of fusion-permissive and fusion-inhibited conditions.

claim: Close inspection of large populations of attached intermediates revealed a sub-category of mitochondria in close contact in which the outer membranes were fused near the rim of the contact region.
source: However, close inspection of large populations of attached intermediates (from 87 high magnification micrographs) by Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) of stained plastic sections revealed a sub-category of mitochondria in close contact, presumably in the docked configuration, in which the outer membranes were fused near the rim of the contact region (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: A docked intermediate was captured with outer membranes of two mitochondria locally fused to form a toroid, 40 nm pore on one side of the contact area.
source: The tomographic volume shows that the outer membranes of two mitochondria were locally fused to form a toroid, 40 nm pore on one side of the contact area (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The toroid pore formed in the path of the docking ring.
source: The toroid pore formed in the path of the docking ring (Figure 6B and Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by 3D reconstruction shown in Figure 6B and Video 4.

claim: Densities in the vicinity of the fusion pore were sparse, suggesting that in this region the docking ring structure was in the process of disassembly.
source: Densities in the vicinity of the fusion pore were sparse, suggesting that in this region the docking ring structure was in the process of disassembly (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of reduced density near the fusion pore.

claim: The docked intermediates are competent for effective outer membrane fusion.
source: These observations provide a proof of principle that the docked intermediates are competent for effective outer membrane fusion, raising the question of which molecular events trigger the transition from docking to outer membrane fusion.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of fusion pores in docked intermediates.

claim: The extent of outer membrane fusion impairment was similar (40 to 50%), irrespective of whether GMP-PNP was added at the beginning or at the end of the 10 min incubation period.
source: Strikingly, the extent of outer membrane fusion impairment was similar (40 to 50%), irrespective of whether GMP-PNP was added at the beginning or at the end of the 10 min incubation period (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: GTP hydrolysis is required for the transition from tethering to docking and for the transition from docking to fusion.
source: Hence, GTP hydrolysis is not only required for the transition from tethering to docking but also for the transition from docking to fusion.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GMP-PNP inhibits fusion regardless of when it is added.

claim: Both the absence or the accumulation of mitofusins inhibits mitochondrial fusion in vivo.
source: To further evaluate the functional relationship between mitofusins, mitochondrial docking and mitochondrial fusion, we took advantage of the fact that both the absence or the accumulation of mitofusins inhibits mitochondrial fusion in vivo (Cohen et al., 2011; Escobar-Henriques et al., 2006; Koshiba et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Absence or 50-fold overexpression of Fzo1 totally abolished respiratory growth at 30°C.
source: Consistent with this, absence or 50-fold overexpression of Fzo1 (Figure 7A; fzo1△ and FZO1 o.e.) totally abolished respiratory growth at 30°C (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: Overexpression of Fzo1 induces a specific phenotype of mitochondrial aggregation.
source: Notably, Fzo1 overexpression also induces a specific phenotype of mitochondrial aggregation (Figure 7C) in which mitochondrial puncta aggregate in one region of the cell cortex (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Overexpression of Fzo1 promotes the attachment of mitochondria to each other.
source: This phenotype suggests that, as well as inhibiting fusion, overexpression of Fzo1 may also promote the attachment of mitochondria to each other.
evidence: This is inferred from the aggregation phenotype observed upon Fzo1 overexpression.

claim: In vitro outer membrane fusion was strongly inhibited but mitochondrial attachment was significantly increased in mitochondria from Fzo1-overexpressing cells.
source: As expected, in vitro outer membrane fusion was strongly inhibited but mitochondrial attachment was significantly increased, with 50% of mitochondria attached to others (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Fzo1 overexpression induced a two-fold increase in mitochondrial attachment both before and after centrifugation.
source: Further analysis indicated that Fzo1 overexpression induced a two-fold increase in mitochondrial attachment both before and after centrifugation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–F.

claim: Mitochondria purified from Fzo1-overexpressing cells retained an increased attachment capacity.
source: Thus, mitochondria purified from Fzo1-overexpressing cells retained an increased attachment capacity, indicating that the in vivo aggregation phenotype (Figure 7C) is caused, at least in part, by perturbations that are intrinsic to outer membranes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the attachment phenotype persists in vitro.

claim: Intermediates with a docking ring were observed less frequently (26%) upon Fzo1 overexpression and the average contact surface was significantly smaller compared to wild-type conditions.
source: While intermediates with a docking ring were formed (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–C), they were observed less frequently (26%) and the average contact surface was significantly smaller compared to docking intermediates observed under wild-type conditions (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data and quantitative analysis shown in Table 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: In 74% of attached intermediates upon Fzo1 overexpression, the surface of apposition was reduced (4970 ± 930 nm²), with outer membranes on average 8.8 ± 0.4 nm apart.
source: In the remaining attached intermediates (74%), the surface of apposition was also reduced (4970 ± 930 nm²), with outer membranes on average 8.8 ± 0.4 nm apart (Figure 7E; blue bracket; Figure 7—figure supplement 2D–E).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 2D–E.

claim: Numerous densities accumulated in regions of closest contact between mitochondria upon Fzo1 overexpression, but the densities were disorganized and did not form globular protein repeats.
source: Importantly, numerous densities accumulated in regions of closest contact between mitochondria (Figure 7F), but the densities were disorganized and did not form globular protein repeats (Figure 7E–F).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data shown in Figure 7E–F.

claim: Attached mitochondria upon Fzo1 overexpression likely correspond to artefactual and abortive fusion intermediates.
source: These attached mitochondria, which were clearly distinct from tethered intermediates observed under wild-type conditions, likely correspond to artefactual and abortive fusion intermediates.
evidence: This is inferred from the disorganized nature of the densities and the fusion defect.

claim: Normal levels of Fzo1 are required for the formation of bona fide docking rings.
source: These results indicate that while normal levels of Fzo1 are required for the formation of bona fide docking rings, overexpression of the mitofusin induces the formation of protein aggregates that perturb the regulated sequence of events required to reach productive mitochondrial docking.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of wild-type and Fzo1-overexpressing conditions.

claim: Overexpression of the mitofusin induces the formation of protein aggregates that perturb the regulated sequence of events required to reach productive mitochondrial docking.
source: These results indicate that while normal levels of Fzo1 are required for the formation of bona fide docking rings, overexpression of the mitofusin induces the formation of protein aggregates that perturb the regulated sequence of events required to reach productive mitochondrial docking.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of disorganized densities and reduced docking upon Fzo1 overexpression.

claim: The units with a defined central density and protrusions extending towards each lipid bilayer bridged the apposed outer membranes.
source: Notably, the units with a defined central density and protrusions extending towards each lipid bilayer bridged the apposed outer membranes (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The units were stabilized in the presence of GMP-PNP.
source: These units were stabilized in the presence of GMP-PNP (Figure 4) and their arrangement may reflect the self-association in trans of a factor extruding from outer membranes (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GMP-PNP treatment increases the proportion of tethered intermediates.

claim: The arrangement of the units may reflect the self-association in trans of a factor extruding from outer membranes.
source: These units were stabilized in the presence of GMP-PNP (Figure 4) and their arrangement may reflect the self-association in trans of a factor extruding from outer membranes (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the morphology of the units.

claim: The observed units are possibly trans-oligomers of Fzo1 molecules.
source: These features thus point to a transmembrane GTPase specialized in connecting outer membranes, raising the possibility that the observed units are indeed trans-oligomers of Fzo1 molecules.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the properties of the units and the known function of Fzo1.

claim: Q-Dots were enriched at the junction of attached FZO1-Avi mitochondria as compared to attached FZO1 mitochondria.
source: While Q-Dots were rarely found on the surface of tagged or untagged mitochondria (Figure 8C and D, right graph), they were enriched at the junction of attached FZO1-Avi mitochondria as compared to attached FZO1 mitochondria (Figure 8D, left graph).
evidence: This is supported by Q-Dot labeling experiments shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: Q-Dots, and therefore the FZO1-Avi constructs, were located either at the periphery of docked contact sites or between tethered contact sites.
source: Moreover, Q-Dots, and therefore the FZO1-Avi constructs, were located either at the periphery of docked contact sites or between tethered contact sites (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-ET data of Q-Dot labeled samples shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The data confirm the accumulation of mitofusins at mitochondrial contact sites.
source: These data confirm the accumulation of mitofusins at mitochondrial contact sites and corroborate the likely contribution of Fzo1 to densities found at junctions of tethered and docked intermediates.
evidence: This is inferred from the Q-Dot labeling experiments showing enrichment of Fzo1 at contact sites.

claim: The data corroborate the likely contribution of Fzo1 to densities found at junctions of tethered and docked intermediates.
source: These data confirm the accumulation of mitofusins at mitochondrial contact sites and corroborate the likely contribution of Fzo1 to densities found at junctions of tethered and docked intermediates.
evidence: This is inferred from the Q-Dot labeling experiments and the morphology of the densities.

claim: Initially outer membranes of two attached mitochondria are tethered by globular protein repeats and membranes approach to within 6 nm.
source: Initially outer membranes of two attached mitochondria are tethered by globular protein repeats and membranes approach to within 6 nm (Figure 9, step 1).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the tethered intermediates.

claim: GTP hydrolysis allows the fusion process to evolve progressively towards mitochondrial docking.
source: Subsequently, GTP hydrolysis allows the fusion process to evolve progressively towards mitochondrial docking (Figure 5), as evidenced by the hybrid intermediates observed upon addition of GMP-PNP two minutes after initiation of tethering (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the time-course experiments with GMP-PNP.

claim: GTP hydrolysis by trans-complexes of atlastins precedes vesicle fusion and is essential to promote tethering of proteoliposomes.
source: Consistent with this, GTP hydrolysis by trans-complexes of atlastins precedes vesicle fusion and is essential to promote tethering of proteoliposomes (Liu et al., 2015; Saini et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on atlastins.

claim: The docked intermediates are characterized by a docking ring of protein density that surrounds extended areas with outer membranes separated by less than 3 nm and devoid of visible densities.
source: The docked intermediates are characterized by a docking ring of protein density that surrounds extended areas with outer membranes separated by less than 3 nm and devoid of visible densities (Figure 9, step 2).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the docked intermediates.

claim: The capture of docked intermediates with partly fused outer membranes demonstrates that docking is the stage that precedes merging of outer membranes.
source: The capture of docked intermediates with partly fused outer membranes, the location of the fusion pore in the path of the docking ring undergoing disassembly and the inhibition of fusion upon treatment of docked mitochondria with GMP-PNP, demonstrates that docking is the stage that precedes merging of outer membranes (Figure 6).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of fusion pores in docked intermediates and the GMP-PNP experiments.

claim: The docking ring of protein densities is the driving force for subsequent bilayer merging.
source: We do not exclude that small protein complexes, which are not visible by cryo-ET, might reside between outer membranes and participate in the fusion process. However, our observations do suggest that the docking ring of protein densities is the driving force for subsequent bilayer merging.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that fusion occurs in the path of the docking ring.

claim: The fusion of bilayers is initiated by further GTP hydrolysis in the path of the docking ring where the outer membrane curvature is most pronounced.
source: We thus propose that the fusion of bilayers is initiated by further GTP hydrolysis in the path of the docking ring where the outer membrane curvature is most pronounced (Figure 9, step 3).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observation of fusion pores at the edge of docking rings.

claim: Further GTP hydrolysis may trigger the disassembly of the docking ring.
source: This step may trigger the disassembly of the docking ring.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observation of reduced density near fusion pores.

claim: Overexpression of Fzo1 inhibited mitochondrial docking and fusion but stimulated the formation of artefactual tethering intermediates characterized by an accumulation of protein aggregates at mitochondrial junctions.
source: Overexpression of Fzo1 inhibited mitochondrial docking and fusion but stimulated the formation of artefactual tethering intermediates that are characterized by an accumulation of protein aggregates at mitochondrial junctions (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Normal levels of mitofusins are required for the formation of the docking rings.
source: This result demonstrates once more that absence of docking correlates with deficient mitochondrial fusion and implies that normal levels of mitofusins are required for the formation of the docking rings.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Fzo1 overexpression reduces docking ring formation.

claim: Increased levels of mitofusins correlate with the accumulation of protein densities at mitochondrial junctions.
source: It is also important to realize that increased levels of mitofusins correlate with the accumulation of protein densities at mitochondrial junctions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of increased densities upon Fzo1 overexpression.

claim: GMP-PNP may bind to mitofusins and inhibit their GTPase activity.
source: GMP-PNP that may bind to mitofusins and inhibit their GTPase activity (Amiott et al., 2009; Ishihara et al., 2004), induced the accumulation of tethered intermediates and prevented progression towards the docked stage (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and experimental data.

claim: Fzo1 enrichment at mitochondrial contact sites was confirmed by Q-dot labeling.
source: Moreover, Fzo1 enrichment at mitochondrial contact sites was confirmed by Q-dot labeling (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by Q-Dot labeling experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: No other GTPase has been shown to be involved in outer membrane fusion.
source: To our knowledge, no other GTPase has been shown to be involved in outer membrane fusion.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge claim based on the literature.

claim: Fzo1 is at least a component of globular protein repeats and docking rings, possibly together with other, as yet unknown factors.
source: In this context, our observations converge to propose that Fzo1 is at least a component of globular protein repeats and docking rings, possibly together with other, as yet unknown factors.
evidence: This is inferred from the multiple lines of evidence pointing to Fzo1 involvement.

claim: The HR2 domain of Mfn1 has been proposed to tether outer membranes at a distance of 16 nm.
source: So far, the only structural insight into mitofusins derives from the HR2 domain of Mfn1 that has been proposed to tether outer membranes at a distance of 16 nm (Koshiba et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The 16 nm membrane spacing proposed for HR2 dimers would exceed the 6 nm membrane spacing measured in tethered intermediates.
source: This would exceed the 6 nm membrane spacing we measured in tethered intermediates.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the HR2 model with the experimental measurements.

claim: The overall morphology of the HR2 dimer can hardly account for the distinctive shape of the protein units observed.
source: The overall morphology of the HR2 dimer can hardly account for the distinctive shape of the protein units we observed.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the HR2 structure with the observed densities.

claim: Mitofusins bound to GMP-PNP or GTP may adopt an open conformation that would promote trans-oligomerization of Fzo1 molecules through their GTPase domain.
source: Similar to BDLP, mitofusins bound to GMP-PNP or GTP may adopt an open conformation that, in analogy to atlastins, would promote trans-oligomerization of Fzo1 molecules through their GTPase domain.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on analogy to BDLP and atlastins.

claim: Conformational changes of the mitofusin oligomers upon GTP hydrolysis would pull the outer membranes closer together.
source: Conformational changes of the mitofusin oligomers upon GTP hydrolysis would pull the outer membranes closer together.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed transition from tethering to docking.

claim: This model is consistent with the shape of the protein units visualized and with the essential requirement of GTP hydrolysis for transition from mitochondrial tethering to mitochondrial docking.
source: This model is not only consistent with the shape of the protein units we visualized but also with the essential requirement of GTP hydrolysis for transition from mitochondrial tethering to mitochondrial docking we unraveled in this study.
evidence: This is stated as support for the proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: An absolute prerequisite for mitochondrial fusion in vivo is that the tips of mitochondrial tubules come close enough to promote attachment between outer membranes.
source: An absolute prerequisite for mitochondrial fusion in vivo is that the tips of mitochondrial tubules come close enough to promote attachment between outer membranes.
evidence: This is stated as a logical requirement for fusion to occur.

claim: In yeast cells, bringing mitochondrial tips close enough requires the participation of actin filaments.
source: In yeast cells, this requires the participation of actin filaments (Simon et al., 1995; Smith et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the in vitro fusion system, the essential role of the cytoskeleton is replaced by centrifugation to bring mitochondria into close enough contact for fusion to proceed.
source: In the in vitro fusion system, the essential role of the cytoskeleton is replaced by centrifugation to bring mitochondria into close enough contact for fusion to proceed (Meeusen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work establishing the in vitro system.

claim: Centrifugation is not sufficient for fusion, and an incubation of at least 10 min on ice is essential for in vitro fusion.
source: However, centrifugation is not sufficient, and an incubation of at least 10 min on ice, previously suggested to promote Fzo1 association in trans, has been shown to be essential for in vitro fusion (Meeusen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Incubation on ice promotes the transition from tethering to docking, which is an active process that requires several rounds of GTP hydrolysis.
source: Our results reveal that incubation on ice promotes the transition from tethering to docking, which is an active process that requires several rounds of GTP hydrolysis to progressively bring opposing outer membranes closer over an extended surface area but is not sufficient for their effective fusion.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing the role of GTP hydrolysis in the transition.

claim: The observation that fusion starts at the edge of the docking ring suggests that the transition from tethering to docking brings membranes closer over an extended area, inducing a locally increased curvature of the lipid bilayer.
source: The observation that fusion starts at the edge of the docking ring and also depends on GTP hydrolysis suggests that the transition from tethering to docking brings membranes closer over an extended area. This would induce a locally increased curvature of the lipid bilayer, which may be critical.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of fusion pores at the edge of docking rings.

claim: An ultimate cycle of GTP hydrolysis in the region of local membrane curvature would lead to fusion instead of bringing membranes closer together.
source: An ultimate cycle of GTP hydrolysis in this region of local membrane curvature would therefore lead to fusion instead of bringing membranes closer together.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the observation of fusion at the edge of docking rings.

claim: The sequence of events shown in Chapter 7 of Don W. Fawcett's 'The Cell' might in fact correspond to successive stages of fusion rather than fission.
source: Notably, micrographs taken from gastric mucosa of a mole, featured in Chapter 7 of Don W. Fawcett's 'The Cell', present a series of three pairs of mitochondria proposed to represent successive stages of mitochondrial fission (Fawcett, 1981). The middle stage intermediate from this series and the fusion events identified in our study actually appear strikingly similar. This not only suggests that the sequence of events shown in this chapter might in fact correspond to successive stages of fusion but also that our model of outer membrane fusion may apply in vivo with mitochondria from mammalian cells.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the similarity between the published micrographs and the current findings.

claim: The model of outer membrane fusion may apply in vivo with mitochondria from mammalian cells.
source: This not only suggests that the sequence of events shown in this chapter might in fact correspond to successive stages of fusion but also that our model of outer membrane fusion may apply in vivo with mitochondria from mammalian cells.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the similarity to published mammalian cell micrographs.

claim: In vivo, the transition from tethering to docking would also involve the action of the cytoskeleton.
source: Whereas in vitro local membrane deformation would be promoted exclusively by successive cycles of GTP hydrolysis after mitochondria become tethered through centrifugation, in vivo the transition from tethering to docking would also involve the action of the cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is inferred from the known role of the cytoskeleton in mitochondrial fusion in vivo.

claim: In the cell, the process of mitochondrial fusion would be regulated by cytoskeletal factors.
source: In the cell, the process of mitochondrial fusion as indicated by our in vitro studies would thus be regulated by cytoskeletal factors.
evidence: This is inferred from the role of the cytoskeleton in bringing mitochondria together in vivo.

claim: Regulation of mitochondrial fusion in vivo involves post-translational modification of mitofusins.
source: Regulation of mitochondrial fusion in vivo also involves post-translational modification of mitofusins (Anton et al., 2011; Cohen et al., 2008; Shutt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In yeast, the efficient fusion of outer membranes requires Fzo1 ubiquitylation by the Mdm30 ubiquitin ligase and subsequent degradation by the proteasome.
source: In yeast, the efficient fusion of outer membranes requires Fzo1 ubiquitylation by the Mdm30 ubiquitin ligase and subsequent degradation by the proteasome (Cohen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: UPS-dependent regulation of Fzo1 was previously shown to take place at the stage of mitochondrial attachment.
source: While its precise function is yet to be fully characterized, this regulation was previously shown to take place at the stage of mitochondrial attachment (Cohen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: It is conceivable that the UPS-dependent regulation of Fzo1 participates in regulating proper assembly of docking rings.
source: It is therefore conceivable that the UPS-dependent regulation of Fzo1 participates in regulating proper assembly of docking rings, which is consistent with the observation that high levels of Fzo1 inhibit mitochondrial docking (Figure 7).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observation that Fzo1 levels affect docking.

claim: Similar mechanisms involving atlastins or OPA1/Mgm1 are likely to be active in the fusion of ER and mitochondrial inner membranes, respectively.
source: Our work provides a detailed dissection of the outer mitochondrial membrane fusion process in vitro and highlights the crucial involvement of Fzo1 in this system. Similar mechanisms involving atlastins or OPA1/Mgm1 are likely to be active in the fusion of ER and mitochondrial inner membranes, respectively.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the similarity of these DRPs to mitofusins.
